summary: Specifies how to use a message authentication code together with an encryption algorithm in the CMS authenticated-enveloped-data content type. This mirrors the encrypt-then-MAC style already used in IPsec, TLS and SSH, and widely supported in crypto libraries.

plainLanguage.summary: To protect a message, you can scramble it and also add a tamper-proof stamp. This describes how to do both together in a standard secure message format.

subtitle: How to encrypt a CMS message and protect it with a MAC, using two keys derived from one master secret.

tldr.problem: CMS had no standard way to combine encryption with integrity protection, even though IPsec, SSL/TLS and SSH already do this, and users expect encryption to also guarantee integrity.
tldr.mechanism: A new authEnc pseudo-algorithm carries one master secret in the RecipientInfo. A pseudorandom function turns it into separate encryption and MAC keys, and the MAC covers the algorithm identifier plus the encrypted content.
tldr.outcome: CMS authenticated-enveloped data can use ordinary encryption and MAC algorithms with existing code. Implementations must take care not to release decrypted data before the MAC is checked.

today: RFC 6476 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the authenticated-enveloped-data type in RFC 5083 and the CMS definition in RFC 5652.

sections.title: Why CMS Needed Authenticated Encryption
sections.content:
RFC 6476 specifies how to use MAC-authenticated encryption with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) authenticated-enveloped-data content type, which is defined in RFC 5083. A MAC (message authentication code) is a short value, computed with a secret key, that shows the data has not been altered.

The RFC points out that session protocols such as IPsec, SSH and TLS already offer integrity-protected encryption. Message-based protocols like CMS did not, although OpenPGP added a form of integrity protection by encrypting a SHA-1 hash of the message alongside the message contents. Usability studies cited in the RFC show that users expect encryption to provide integrity protection, which causes problems when it does not.
sections.plainLanguage: Locking a note in a box keeps it private, but people also assume nobody changed it. This RFC adds a seal so that assumption is actually true.

sections.title: One Master Secret, Two Keys
sections.content:
Ordinary CMS encryption uses a content-encryption key (CEK) to encrypt the payload, and the CEK is in turn encrypted by a key-encryption key (KEK). Authenticated encryption needs two keys, one for encryption and one for authentication. The RFC uses a pseudorandom function (PRF) to turn a single block of keying material into both.

So the usual KEK( CEK ) || CEK( data ) becomes KEK( master_secret ) || MAC( CEK( data ) ). The MAC key and the encryption key are derived from the master secret with the strings "authentication" and "encryption".

Using the PRF step matters. If the whole exchanged key were used for encryption and only a hash of it for the MAC, an attacker could strip the outer MAC layer and rewrite the envelope back to plain EnvelopedData or EncryptedData. With the PRF in the middle, any such rollback attempt ends in a decryption failure.

The PRF chosen is PBKDF2, because it is already used in CMS. The RFC notes that a universal PRF such as HKDF could later be substituted by naming it in the prfAlgorithm field.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine one magic seed that grows two different keys, one for the lock and one for the seal. Because both come from the same seed, an attacker cannot remove the seal and pretend the box was never sealed.

sections.title: The authEnc Pseudo-Algorithm
sections.content:
The mechanism lives inside the existing CMS RecipientInfo framework. A new pseudo-algorithm called authEnc stands in place of a single combined encrypt-and-hash algorithm. The RecipientInfo then carries a master secret instead of, say, an AES or HMAC-SHA1 key.

There are two forms: id-alg-authEnc-128 conveys 128 bits of keying material and id-alg-authEnc-256 conveys 256 bits. Their object identifiers are { id-alg 15 } and { id-alg 16 }. The RFC offers two sizes because users asked for AES-256 next to AES-128, and says that allowing arbitrary lengths would add complexity for no benefit.

The parameters name the three algorithms involved: prfAlgorithm (optional, default PBKDF2), encAlgorithm and macAlgorithm. By default PBKDF2 uses HMAC-SHA1. Since only the PRF part is wanted, the PBKDF2 salt is an empty string and the iterationCount is one, which turns the key derivation function into a pure PRF. Those two values encode as 08 00 02 01 01.

For other PRFs, the RFC says extra parameters such as salts, tags and identification strings SHOULD be empty and any iteration count SHOULD be one. If the MAC key size is ambiguous, it is RECOMMENDED to state it in the macAlgorithm identifier or in a separate standards document.
sections.plainLanguage: The message carries a note saying which lock, which seal and which key-maker were used. The key-maker is told to use only its plain recipe, with no extra spices.

sections.title: Processing a Message
sections.content:
The sender generates a random master secret and sends it to each recipient through the RecipientInfo. From it, two keys are derived: MAC-K using "authentication" and Enc-K using "encryption", each with an iteration count of 1.

The content is then processed as a union of EncryptedData and AuthenticatedData. The special rule is that the ContentEncryptionAlgorithmIdentifier is MACed together with the encrypted content, so the nesting is MAC( contentEncrAlgoID || encrypt( content ) ). If authenticated attributes are present, they are MACed after the encrypted content.

Covering the algorithm identifier is deliberate. Otherwise an attacker could tamper with the encryption parameters, for example the IV, and change the decrypted output without the MAC check on the ciphertext noticing. The identifier is MACed exactly as encoded, with no conversion to a canonical form such as DER.

The RFC calls the chosen order encrypt-and-authenticate and says it is the more secure option compared with authenticate-and-encrypt.
sections.plainLanguage: First scramble the message, then put a seal over the scrambled message and over the instructions for unscrambling it. That way nobody can quietly change the instructions.

sections.title: Test Vectors and S/MIME Capabilities
sections.content:
The RFC gives two sample messages for checking an implementation. Both use the password "password" through CMS PasswordRecipientInfo, the 128-bit authEnc128 form and HMAC-SHA1. One uses triple DES and the other uses AES. Triple DES is used first because its short block size makes it easier to corrupt chosen bytes in CBC mode for testing, which gives a correct decryption but a failed MAC check.

For the triple DES message, corrupting a byte at positions 192-208 tests payload corruption detection, and positions 168-174 test metadata corruption detection.

An S/MIME client SHOULD announce support through the SMIMECapabilities attribute. To advertise MAC-authenticated encryption it MUST include the authEnc128 and/or authEnc256 identifier with algorithm parameters absent. The MAC and encryption algorithms are chosen from the other entries in the attribute or by mutual agreement.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC includes practice messages so builders can check their work, and a way for mail programs to say "I understand this new kind of sealed box."

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Unlike SignedData or AuthenticatedData, the primary job of this mechanism is encryption, so decryption can succeed while the MAC that follows the ciphertext later fails. A streaming implementation may emit plaintext before it has read and checked the MAC, and users could act on data that turns out to be tainted.

A second risk is truncation. An overly helpful implementation might treat missing trailing data as harmless, letting an attacker cut the message before the MAC value and defeat authentication.

The suggested mitigations are to buffer the whole message and verify the MAC before decrypting, or to split long messages into smaller ones that can each be processed atomically. If neither is possible, implementations should make it obvious that an authentication failure happened and that earlier output must not be used. Any data-formatting problem, such as truncated or missing trailing data, should be treated as a MAC verification failure.
sections.plainLanguage: If you open a package before checking the seal, you might use something that was tampered with. So check the seal first, and treat a torn package as a failed check.
